description: Why we cook food, how heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation, and choosing methods to conserve nutrients.
content_html:
Why Do We Cook Food?

Most food can be eaten raw, but cooking transforms it in ways that make it safer, tastier and more nutritious. There are five core reasons why we cook food, and the written paper expects you to know all of them.

First, cooking makes food safe to eat. Raw chicken can harbour dangerous bacteria. When a chicken breast reaches a core temperature of 75°C, the heat kills pathogenic microorganisms and the meat becomes safe. Second, cooking develops flavours. A raw onion is sharp and pungent; fry it slowly and the sugars caramelise, creating a sweet, golden depth that no raw onion can match. Third, cooking improves texture. Raw potato is starchy and hard; boiling it gelatinises the starch and softens the cell walls, giving it the floury texture we expect. Fourth, cooking improves shelf life. Blanching vegetables before freezing destroys the enzymes that cause spoilage, extending how long the food stays usable. Fifth, cooking gives variety in the diet — the same chicken breast can be poached, roasted, grilled or stir-fried, each method producing a different colour, flavour and texture.

Key Fact

The five reasons food is cooked: make food safe; develop flavours; improve texture; improve shelf life; give variety in the diet. All five are expected in the written paper.

How Heat Is Transferred to Food

Heat does not simply “jump” into food — it travels by one of three distinct mechanisms: conduction, convection, and radiation. Understanding which mechanism is at work in a given cooking method is a high-tariff skill.

Conduction

Conduction happens when heat passes through direct contact, molecule to molecule. Place a frying pan on a hob. The burner heats the metal base of the pan; the molecules at the bottom vibrate faster and pass their energy along to neighbouring molecules. The heat travels upward through the pan until the cooking surface is hot enough to fry. When you lay a chicken breast into the hot pan, conduction transfers heat from the pan surface into the meat. Metals are good conductors — this is why a metal frying pan heats quickly. Food itself is a poor conductor, which is why the centre of a thick piece of meat takes much longer to cook than the outside.

Convection

Convection relies on the movement of a fluid — either liquid or gas. When you heat a pan of water, the water at the bottom nearest the heat source warms first, becomes less dense, and rises. Cooler water from the top falls to replace it, setting up a circulation known as a convection current. This is why a sauce heats unevenly if you leave it still — only the bottom is directly heated by conduction, and without stirring, the top stays cool. Agitation — stirring with a wooden spoon or whisk — forces the hot liquid to mix evenly with the cooler liquid, distributing the heat throughout the sauce. In an oven, hot air rises and circulates in the same way; a fan-assisted oven speeds this up by moving the air artificially.

When you make a béchamel sauce, conduction heats the milk and roux from below, while convection currents try to circulate the liquid. However, starch granules can settle at the bottom and scorch before the top of the sauce even heats through. Stirring constantly does two things: it breaks up the convection pattern so all the sauce heats evenly, and it keeps the starch granules suspended so they don’t stick and burn. Without agitation, the starch at the bottom scorches while the top stays raw — you end up with a lumpy, bitter sauce. This is why the spec specifically lists “the need for agitation” when cooking a sauce.

Radiation

Radiation transfers heat as infrared waves, which do not need any medium — they travel through air just as sunlight travels through space. The grill in an oven is the clearest classroom example. When you place halloumi or tomatoes under a grill, the glowing element emits infrared radiation that travels downward, striking the surface of the food and heating it directly. No air needs to move; no contact is required. This is why the top surface of grilled bread toasts and browns rapidly while the underside stays pale until turned over. Radiation browns and chars surfaces in a way that conduction and convection alone cannot.

Key Fact

Conduction: heat passes through direct contact (frying pan to food). Convection: heat moves through circulating currents in liquid or gas (boiling water, oven air). Radiation: heat travels as infrared waves (grill browning a surface).

Selecting the Right Cooking Method

Choosing a cooking method is not just about taste — it also affects the nutritional value and palatability of the finished dish. The spec groups cooking methods into three families:

Water-based methods include steaming, boiling, simmering, blanching, poaching and braising. These use water or steam as the heat-transfer medium. Boiling and simmering use convection currents to heat food evenly throughout. Steaming keeps food above boiling water, so heat reaches it by convection in the steam. Because the food is not submerged, fewer water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C and the B vitamins) leach out — steaming is therefore generally better than boiling for preserving water-soluble vitamins.

Dry methods include baking, roasting, grilling and dry frying. These use hot air (convection) or direct heat (radiation or conduction) without added water or fat. Grilling uses radiation from above; baking and roasting rely on convection in hot oven air. Because no water is present, browning reactions such as dextrinisation (bread crust) and caramelisation (roasted carrots) occur more readily, improving colour and flavour.

Fat-based methods include shallow frying and stir-frying. A small amount of oil is used in the pan; conduction transfers heat from the hot pan surface through the oil to the food. Stir-frying uses very high heat and constant movement over a short time, which preserves texture and much of the vitamin C content of vegetables because the cooking time is brief.

This is a very common misconception. Nutrient loss depends on three factors: temperature, cooking time and whether the food is submerged in water. Water-soluble vitamins (C and B group) leach into cooking water — this is why boiling a broccoli floret for ten minutes destroys most of its vitamin C. Steaming, microwaving or stir-frying the same broccoli for two to three minutes retains far more. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) are not lost into water but can be destroyed by very high temperatures over long cooking times. The nutritional impact of a cooking method depends on which vitamins the food contains and how the method treats water-soluble versus fat-soluble nutrients differently.

Marinades and Palatability

Cooking also affects the palatability of food — its overall pleasantness in terms of appearance, colour, flavour, texture, smell and mouthfeel. One specific technique in this area is the use of marinades. When a chicken thigh sits overnight in a yoghurt and lemon juice marinade, the acid in the lemon juice begins to denature the protein in the surface layer of the meat. The protein chains unravel, the texture softens, and the flavours from the marinade penetrate more deeply. When the chicken is then cooked, the denatured protein coagulates and sets in a more flavourful, more tender state than an unmarinated piece would. Acids in marinades (lemon juice, vinegar, wine) are not just for flavour — they are doing chemical work on the protein structure before the heat even begins.
exam_tip_html: Questions on this topic often use the command word Explain, which means “give reasons for and/or causes of” — you must link cause and effect using words like ‘because’, ‘this means that’ or ‘as a result’. A very common error on a 4-mark Explain question about heat transfer is to name the method without explaining the mechanism. Writing “the sauce is heated by convection” earns one mark at most; writing “the sauce is heated by convection because the hot liquid at the bottom becomes less dense and rises, forcing cooler liquid down — this sets up a circulation current that gradually warms the whole sauce” earns the full marks. For a 6-mark Explain question asking you to compare cooking methods for their effect on nutritive value, structure your answer around two or three methods with developed reasons, not a list of bullet points. The marker is looking for the word ‘because’ and a named outcome (e.g. “steaming retains more vitamin C because the broccoli is not submerged, so fewer water-soluble vitamins leach into the cooking water”).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Food is cooked for five reasons: safety, flavour development, improved texture, extended shelf life and dietary variety — learn all five.
  • Heat reaches food by conduction (direct contact), convection (circulating currents in liquid or gas) or radiation (infrared waves from a grill — no medium needed). Agitation is essential when cooking a sauce to distribute heat evenly by convection.
  • Method choice affects nutrients: steaming and stir-frying conserve more water-soluble vitamins than boiling; marinades use acid to denature and tenderise protein before cooking begins.

practice_questions.text:
Which method of heat transfer involves the movement of circulating currents within a liquid?
A. Conduction
B. Convection
C. Radiation
D. Evaporation
Name two reasons why food is cooked.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each valid reason (any two from): make food safe to eat; develop flavours; improve texture; improve shelf life; give variety in the diet.

practice_questions.text: Describe how heat is transferred to food when it is placed under a grill.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: identification of radiation as the mechanism (1); explanation that the grill element emits infrared waves (1); statement that infrared travels without a medium and heats the surface of the food directly (1). Credit also: the surface browns/chars rapidly because radiation acts directly on the food surface (1) in place of any of the above.

practice_questions.text: Priya is making a beef stew for her family. She decides to braise the beef in stock on the hob rather than dry-roasting it in the oven. Explain why braising in liquid might be a better choice for preserving the tenderness of the beef.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: braising uses a water-based method where the beef is partially submerged in liquid (1); convection currents in the hot stock circulate heat around the meat gently and evenly (1); the low, sustained temperature over a long time breaks down the tough collagen in the beef into gelatine, making it tender (1); dry-roasting uses higher temperatures and dry heat, which can tighten (coagulate) the protein fibres and make the meat tough if overcooked (1).

practice_questions.text:
Luca is a year 10 student preparing a vegetable stir-fry and a vegetable soup as two dishes for a cookery assessment. He is thinking about which cooking method best preserves the vitamin C content of his broccoli and red pepper.

Explain how the choice of cooking method affects the vitamin C content of vegetables, and recommend which method Luca should use for maximum retention of vitamin C. Give reasons for your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear identification that vitamin C is water-soluble and leaches into cooking water; developed explanation of why boiling/simmering causes significant vitamin C loss (long contact with water, heat); clear explanation of why stir-frying retains more vitamin C (very high heat for a short time, no water, food moves quickly through the pan); recommendation of stir-fry with a supported reason; accurate use of food-science vocabulary (water-soluble, leach, denaturation of cell walls); applied to Luca's specific dishes.
Secure (3-4 marks): Correct identification that boiling causes vitamin C loss; some explanation of why; recommendation made but reasoning is partial or not fully linked to Luca's context.
Developing (2 marks): Relevant points about cooking affecting vitamins but limited development; may state stir-frying is better without explaining why.
Emerging (1 mark): Basic point such as 'boiling destroys vitamins' with no further explanation.

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which marinating meat in an acid-based marinade changes the meat before it is cooked.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each valid point (any two from): the acid denatures the protein in the surface layer, unfolding the protein chains; the texture of the meat softens/tenderises; flavours from the marinade penetrate more deeply into the meat; moisture from the marinade is absorbed, keeping the meat juicier during cooking.

knowledge_checks.q: A student is making a bechamel sauce on the hob. She leaves it without stirring and the bottom burns while the top stays cool. Which statement best explains why stirring is essential?
options: Stirring speeds up conduction through the pan base.
Stirring distributes the convection currents so all the sauce heats evenly.
Stirring causes radiation to penetrate the sauce from above.
Stirring prevents the sauce from reaching boiling point.

knowledge_checks.q: Which cooking method best conserves the water-soluble vitamin C content of broccoli?
options: Boiling in a large pan of water for 10 minutes
Steaming over boiling water for 4 minutes

knowledge_checks.q: Heat travels from a grill element to the surface of food without any medium, as _____ waves.
When cooking a sauce, _____ is needed to distribute heat evenly and prevent the starch from scorching at the bottom of the pan.
Match each cooking method to the primary heat transfer mechanism it uses.
left: Hob in a saucepan of boiling water
Metal frying pan surface heating a fish fillet

flashcard_questions.q: What are the five reasons food is cooked?
flashcard_questions.a: Safety, develop flavours, improve texture, improve shelf life, give variety.

flashcard_questions.q: In heat transfer, what is conduction?
flashcard_questions.a: Heat passing from molecule to molecule through direct contact.

flashcard_questions.q: In heat transfer, what is convection?
flashcard_questions.a: Heat moving through circulating currents in a liquid or gas.

flashcard_questions.q: In heat transfer, what is radiation?
flashcard_questions.a: Heat travelling as infrared waves, needing no medium.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must a white sauce be stirred constantly while heating?
flashcard_questions.a: To distribute convection currents evenly and prevent starch from scorching.

flashcard_questions.q: Which heat transfer method browns the surface of halloumi under a grill?
Why does steaming preserve more vitamin C than boiling?
flashcard_questions.a: Food is not submerged, so fewer water-soluble vitamins leach into the water.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of vitamins are lost when vegetables are boiled in water?
flashcard_questions.a: Water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C and B vitamins).

flashcard_questions.q: What chemical process does an acid marinade begin on the surface of meat?
flashcard_questions.a: Denaturation — the acid unravels protein chains, softening the texture.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two dry cooking methods from the spec.
flashcard_questions.a: Baking and grilling (also accept roasting or dry frying).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does stir-frying retain more vitamin C than boiling?
flashcard_questions.a: Very high heat for a short time with no cooking water.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of agitation when cooking a sauce on the hob?
flashcard_questions.a: It forces hot and cool liquid to mix, distributing heat evenly.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the centre of a thick piece of meat take longer to cook than the outside?
flashcard_questions.a: Food is a poor conductor, so heat travels slowly through its depth.

glossary_terms.definition: The transfer of heat through direct contact between molecules, passing energy from particle to particle without movement of the material itself.
The transfer of heat through the movement of a fluid (liquid or gas), where hotter, less dense material rises and cooler material sinks, creating a circulating current.
The transfer of heat energy as electromagnetic waves (infrared radiation), which travel without needing any medium and heat the surface of food directly.
Vitamins that dissolve in water and cannot be stored in the body, including vitamin C and all the B vitamins, which are easily lost when food is cooked in water.
A seasoned liquid, often containing an acid such as lemon juice, vinegar or yoghurt, in which food is soaked before cooking to add flavour, moisture and sometimes to tenderise the proteins.
The unfolding of a protein's three-dimensional structure caused by heat, acid, salt or mechanical action, permanently changing the protein's shape and properties.
